extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (PR managers, researchers, activists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying publics (environmental, consumer, minority), designing objectives, and evaluating public relations programs using the situational theory and communication-objective approaches. Emphasis on how to measure publics, media behavior, and program outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situational theory diagnostic variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure problem recognition, level of involvement, and constraint recognition for issues to identify publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers measured problem recognition, level of involvement, and constraint recognition for multiple issues and used a statistical procedure to identify publics. These three concepts are the core situational-theory variables used to classify publics and predict communication behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-category public typology (basic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publics fall into one of four kinds: publics active on all related issues; publics apathetic on all related issues; publics active only on an issue or a small number of issues that involve nearly everyone in the population; publics active only on single issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this typology to anticipate the scope of concern a public will have and to segment audiences for PR programs. The typology underpins later statistical classification of publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral-molecule / consumer-decision steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Segments of the behavioral molecule (Detect... Construct... Define... Select... Confirm... Behave... Detect...) map to consumer decision steps: developing a need (detect); searching/comparing alternatives (construct/define); purchasing (behave); postpurchase (second detect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these steps to design consumer-targeted information for each decision stage. The consumer decision model aligns with situational theory to predict which publics will seek information and use consumer programs (e.g., unit pricing, open dating).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publics classification by involvement/problem/constraint (empirical types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirically derived publics include: general environmentalist (high problem recognition & involvement; low constraint recognition), involving-issue public (high involvement/problem recognition but feel constrained), apathetic public (low problem recognition & involvement; high constraint recognition), and special-issue publics (e.g., air pollution, superhighway, whale publics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistical analyses can reveal 4–5 publics in samples; these publics have predictable demographic profiles and information/communication behaviors useful for targeting campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic and behavioral indicators of activist publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Activist (general environmentalist) publics tend to be young, white, college-educated, in upper occupational classes, politically liberal, cosmopolitan, and more likely to use specialized environmental media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these demographic indicators to profile and target likely activists; note that involvement can vary by issue and local context (e.g., rural vs urban differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Involvement effect on apathetic publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Apathetic publics become more aware and active when an environmental/consumer/minority issue directly involves them; however, when self-interest is threatened (e.g., potential job loss), they often oppose environmentalist positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan messaging recognizing that personal stakes and perceived constraints shape whether people act on their expressed concerns; anticipate opposition when regulation threatens jobs or local economic interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental media coverage characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass media have increased coverage of environmental issues but generally cover them superficially and are dependent on staged events; specialized environmental reporters do more enterprise reporting, while local media often avoid exposing polluters in their circulation area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect media attention primarily for staged events, reports, press conferences, or national policy stories; tailor PR tactics accordingly (e.g., staging, providing newsworthy reports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-event dependence and activist media tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Because reporters 'wait for it to happen,' activists use staged events (protests, Earth Day, press conferences) to generate media coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use staged, newsworthy actions to attract superficial mass-media coverage; for sustained or investigative coverage, target specialized reporters or national outlets with enterprise capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental Afghanistanism (media avoidance of local polluters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Local newspapers tend to report environmental problems 'in the community up the road' and avoid exposing local polluters; coverage often emphasizes generalities and polls rather than actionable information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking local exposure of pollution, expect resistance; consider external or national venues or build community-level evidence and events that overcome local media avoidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude-and-behavior (domino) objective model
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional PR objectives concentrate on attitude and behavioral objectives: messages topple the knowledge domino, which topples the attitude domino, which topples the behavior domino.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns this asymmetric domino model 'doesn't work well' for activist-related programs; while common, these objectives are difficult to achieve for environmental/consumer/minority issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication objective (symmetric model) and evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: For symmetric programs developed for activist publics, the communication objective should have first priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate communication objectives by counting: the number of contacts your organization makes with members of the opposing side; articles telling your side that appear in environmental/consumer/minority media; contacts with government officials in regulatory agencies. Also measure message retention and hedging as communication effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hedging and wedging belief constructs
rubrics_metrics.description: Two major belief types identified: 'reversal of trends' (solve problems by reversing resource-use trends) and 'functional substitutes' (replace scarce resources with equivalents). Environmental publics may 'hedge' reversal-of-trends positions with functional-substitutes reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure hedging as a communication objective (e.g., evidence that publics combine environmental and economic beliefs). Activists hedge when personally involved; industry seeks to induce hedging by emphasizing substitutes or economic arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing consumer PR using situational variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumer publics and their use of consumer information can be predicted by problem recognition and constraint recognition: those who detect a problem and feel unconstrained will go through the full decision process and be active information seekers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment consumer publics (e.g., working-class constrained by transportation; professionals constrained by time; middle-class blue-collar problem-facing) and tailor consumer-information programs (unit pricing, open dating, labeling) to likely users and information channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minority publics: constraint recognition and program implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Minority publics (e.g., black publics) are likely to exhibit high levels of constraint recognition, producing constrained- or fatalistic-behavior categories even when problems are perceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minority relations programs should prioritize community participation and programs that remove constraints (e.g., affirmative-action contracts). Expect both constrained activism and cases where minorities form high-involvement publics on issues directly affecting them (e.g., job discrimination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Research/evaluation procedures for identifying publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure situational variables for multiple issues (examples: air pollution, energy shortage, strip mining, superhighways, oil spills, pesticides, nuclear power) and apply statistical procedures to classify publics and reveal patterns (e.g., which issues produce single-issue publics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interviews/surveys across urban and rural samples, compare problem recognition/involvement/constraint across issues, and use clustering/factor analysis to derive public segments and tailor strategies accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of coorientational and other evaluative methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Coorientational methods (discussed in other chapters) and measures like message retention, hedging, and counts of contacts/articles can be used to evaluate PR objectives and programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine quantitative counts (contacts, articles) with attitude/cognition measures (hedging, belief constructs) and coorientation to assess whether programs have shifted perceptions or relationships between organizations and publics.
